We learned yesterday that a judge allowed a $32 billion lawsuit to proceed alleging that Apple Photos’ facial recognition feature violates a state privacy law.

Although the two companies sit at opposite ends of the privacy spectrum, the case has been conflated with Meta’s use of facial recognition. In allowing the case to proceed, the court fundamentally failed to understand how the feature works…

The earlier allegations against Meta

To properly understand the situation, we need to start with a lawsuit against Meta that dates back to 2015.

Because the facial recognition was performed on Meta’s servers, and Meta was able to identify those faces, the company did break the law, and was ultimately forced to settle the claims for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under the same Illinois statute — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which states that companies cannot collect biometric data without consent.

Apple’s approach is entirely different

There is a huge problem with the allegation: Apple absolutely did not collect biometric data in order to perform facial recognition in its Apple Photos app. As Apple pointed out in a 2021 machine learning research paper, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

What’s more, the iPhone only goes as far as “these people in these photos appear to be the same person” — it has no idea who that person is. Only the iPhone user themselves is able to give them a name.

Apple’s Photos privacy policy reflects this too.

This lawsuit has been bouncing around the legal system for six years now, yet it takes only a few minutes of research to find that its allegations are plainly wrong — something which I find astonishing.

Courts and legislators should be actively championing Apple’s approach to privacy protection, rather than conflating it with the privacy-destructive practices of companies like Meta.

This is yet another example of courts and legislators simply not understanding the technology they are attempting to regulate. The most obvious example, of course, is end-to-end encryption. Multiple countries have threatened or even attempted to ban it, despite having no clue how it actually works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians cannot be experts in every field. But they do have access to experts, and what I find baffling is that lawsuits and legislative attempts with such obvious fundamental errors can proceed for years without anyone pointing out the problems.
